connection: Sessions 21–22 created IEnumerable-based LINQ pipelines. The test project still contains its template placeholder, so this session replaces that placeholder with focused tests that make deferred execution and ToList snapshots observable.
objectives: Predict when an IEnumerable query executes.
Prove that a deferred query can observe source changes made before enumeration.
Use ToList when a fixed snapshot is actually required.
Recognize IQueryable as a later database-provider variation without memorizing it now.

visuals.title: GetEmployeeClockEntries returns an unevaluated query
visuals.explanation: IEnumerable<ClockEntry> is a promise, not a result -- the real Where clause has not run yet when GetEmployeeClockEntries returns.

visuals.title: .Sum() is what actually triggers execution
visuals.explanation: CalculateTotalHours's .Sum() call is the real point where GetEmployeeClockEntries's deferred query is finally enumerated.

visuals.title: .ToList() forces a fixed snapshot
visuals.explanation: DeferredEntryQuery.Completed(entries).ToList() materializes immediately -- later changes to entries will not affect the snapshot.

visuals.title: IQueryable defers to a provider, not just to enumeration
visuals.explanation: Session 31-32's EF Core queries return IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> -- the same deferred principle, translated to SQL instead of run in-process.

preQuiz.prompt: When does GetEmployeeClockEntries's Where clause actually run?
options: When the returned IEnumerable<ClockEntry> is enumerated (a foreach, ToList, or Sum) -- not when GetEmployeeClockEntries itself is called
Never -- Where is evaluated at compile time
preQuiz.explanation: IEnumerable's Where is deferred: calling GetEmployeeClockEntries builds a query description, and CalculateTotalHours's .Sum() is what actually walks _clockEntries and applies the filter.

preQuiz.prompt: If a new ClockEntry is added to _clockEntries after GetEmployeeClockEntries returns but before .Sum() enumerates it, what happens?
options: The new entry can be included in the sum, since the query re-reads the live list at enumeration time
The new entry is guaranteed to be excluded
preQuiz.explanation: Deferred execution means the query is a live view over _clockEntries at the moment it is enumerated, not a snapshot taken when GetEmployeeClockEntries was called.

preQuiz.prompt: What does .ToList() do differently from just holding an IEnumerable<ClockEntry> reference?
options: It forces immediate enumeration and copies matching elements into a new List, fixed at that moment
It changes the Where clause's filtering logic
It converts the query into an IQueryable
preQuiz.explanation: ToList materializes: it runs the deferred query right now and returns a stable snapshot that later changes to the source will not affect.

concept.title: GetEmployeeClockEntries returns a query, not a list
paragraphs: The real method's return type is IEnumerable<ClockEntry> -- a promise of a sequence, not the sequence itself. The .Where() call inside it builds that promise but does not walk _clockEntries yet.
CalculateTotalHours is what actually triggers execution, because .Sum() has to enumerate every element to add it up.

concept.title: ToList forces evaluation now
paragraphs: DeferredEntryQuery.Completed returns an IEnumerable<ClockEntry> that has not run yet. Calling .ToList() on it walks _clockEntries immediately and returns a fixed List<ClockEntry> snapshot.

The difference is observable: if the source list changes after the deferred query was built but before it is enumerated, an un-materialized IEnumerable can see the change; a .ToList() snapshot cannot.

concept.title: IQueryable defers differently: to a provider, not just to enumeration
paragraphs: GetEmployeeClockEntries's IEnumerable<ClockEntry> runs entirely in this process, in plain C#. Session 31-32's EF Core queries return IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> instead: LINQ builds an expression tree that a database provider translates into SQL only when enumerated.
Same deferred-until-enumerated principle, different execution target -- in-process C# versus a translated database query.

lab.objective: Use permanent tests to prove deferred query behavior and materialized snapshot behavior.
lab.startingCondition: Session 21 introduced production IEnumerable-based LINQ queries. The test project exists but contains only its template placeholder.
steps: Open tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/UnitTest1.cs and confirm it contains only the unused xUnit template test.
In DeferredExecutionTests.cs, declare a public sealed class named DeferredExecutionTests.
In DeferredQuery_SeesValuesAddedBeforeEnumeration, create a List<int> variable named source containing 1 and 2.
Call Where on source to keep even values, store the returned query in IEnumerable<int> evens, and do not enumerate it yet.
Add 4 to source after the evens query has been created.
Assert that enumerating evens produces 2 and 4.
Add a second Fact method named MaterializedQuery_DoesNotChangeWithSource.
In MaterializedQuery_DoesNotChangeWithSource, create a new List<int> variable named source containing 1 and 2.
Call Where on the second source to keep even values.
Call ToList immediately and store the resulting List<int> in a variable named snapshot.
Add 4 to the second source after snapshot has been created.
Assert that snapshot still contains only 2.
Add a short comment above evens stating that Where creates a deferred query.
Add a short comment above snapshot stating that ToList runs the query and stores its current results.

steps.text: Run the Domain.Tests project, then test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln. Open the existing solution reveal only after writing both tests.

dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

commit: session-23: teach deferred execution and materialization
review: The lab uses tests because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does CalculateTotalHours never need to call .ToList() on the result of GetEmployeeClockEntries?
options: It only enumerates the sequence once (inside .Sum()), so there is no benefit to materializing a separate snapshot first
postQuiz.explanation: Materializing is worth the extra allocation when a sequence will be enumerated more than once, or when you need a stable snapshot -- CalculateTotalHours does neither.

postQuiz.prompt: What is the risk of enumerating the same un-materialized deferred query twice in a row (e.g. once to count, once to sum)?
options: The underlying Where/filter logic re-runs both times, which is wasted work and, for a database-backed IQueryable, a second round trip
The second enumeration always throws an exception
There is no risk; deferred queries are cached automatically after the first enumeration
postQuiz.explanation: Deferred execution means every enumeration re-runs the query from scratch -- exactly why Session 31-32's EF Core queries call .ToListAsync() once and reuse the materialized result.

postQuiz.prompt: Once Session 31 introduces IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity>, what changes about where the Where clause actually executes?
options: The database provider translates the Where clause into SQL and executes it in the database, not in this process
Nothing changes -- IQueryable behaves identically to IEnumerable
The Where clause runs at compile time instead of runtime
postQuiz.explanation: This is the concrete difference Session 32 explores: IEnumerable filters in-process C# objects; IQueryable's expression tree is translated and executed by the database provider.

reflections: Why does GetEmployeeClockEntries's deferred IEnumerable<ClockEntry> behave differently from a materialized List<ClockEntry> if _clockEntries changes between the call and the enumeration?
When would you deliberately call .ToList() on GetEmployeeClockEntries's result, even though CalculateTotalHours does not?
What concrete difference will Session 32 show between this session's in-process IEnumerable queries and EF Core's IQueryable queries?
whatBreaks: Calling .ToList() unnecessarily inside GetEmployeeClockEntries would force evaluation before the caller decides what to do with the result, silently changing its behavior from a live view to a fixed snapshot. Enumerating a deferred query multiple times when the underlying provider is a database (Session 32) means multiple round trips, not one. Confusing IEnumerable's in-process execution with IQueryable's provider-translated execution leads to assuming SQL-level operations (like case-insensitive collation) that only IQueryable's translation actually provides.
summary: Session 23 proves execution timing with two small permanent tests: Where remains deferred until enumeration, while ToList executes immediately and returns a snapshot. IQueryable remains only a brief preview for the later EF Core sessions.
